children.text: § 777. āha, yadi vipāko ’nubhavaḥ pratijñāyate, tatkarmānubhūtaṃ sat, kim ābharaṇavadavatiṣṭhate āhosvin niṣpītasāraṃ pracyavate? ity atrocyate —
children.translated_text: Section 777. One asks: if fruition (<s>vipāka</s>) is accepted as experience, then when that karma has been experienced, does it remain like an ornament, or does it fall away once its essence is exhausted? To this it is replied —

children.text: tataś ca nirjarā ||
children.translated_text: And from that, <s>nirjarā</s> (shedding of karma).

children.text: § 778. pīḍānugrahāv ātmane pradāyābhyavahṛṭaudanādivikāravatpūrvasthitikṣayād avasthānābhāvāt karmaṇo nivṛttir nirjarā. sā dviprakārā — vipākajā itarā ca. tatra caturgatāv anekajātiviśeṣāvaghūrṇite saṃsāramahārṇave ciraṃ paribhramataḥ śubhāśubhasya karmaṇaḥ krameṇa paripākakālaprāptasyānubhavodayāvalisroto ’nupravaviṣṭasyārabdhaphalasya yā nivṛttiḥ sā vipākajā nirjarā. yatkarmāprāptavipākakālam aupakramikakriyāviśeṣasāmarthyād anudīrṇaṃ balād udīryodayāvaliṃ praveśya vedyate āmrapanasādipākavat sā avipākajā nirjarā. ’ca’ śabdo nimittāntarasamuccayārthaḥ. ‘tapasā nirjarā ca’ iti vakṣyate tataś ca bhavati anyataś ceti sūtrārtho yojitaḥ. kim artham iha nirjarānirdeśaḥ kriyate, saṃvarāt parā nirdeṣṭavyā uddeśavat? laghvartham iha vacanam. tatra hi pāṭhe ‘vipāko ’nubhavaḥ’ iti punar anuvādaḥ kartavyaḥ syāt.
children.translated_text: Section 778. Having given affliction and benefit to the soul, like the transformation of consumed food and the like, karma ceases due to the expiry of its previously [determined] duration and the absence of [further] continuance — this cessation is <s>nirjarā</s> (shedding). It is of two kinds: arising from fruition (<s>vipākajā</s>) and the other [kind]. In the case of the first, as [the soul] wanders long in the great ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>, revolving through the four destinies and innumerable species, the wholesome and unwholesome karma whose time of ripening has gradually arrived, which has entered the stream of the series of fruition-rise, and whose fruit has commenced — its cessation is <s>nirjarā</s> arising from fruition. The karma whose time of fruition has not arrived but which, through the power of special deliberate practices, though not yet risen, is forcibly made to rise and brought into the series of fruition-rise and experienced — like the [forced] ripening of mangoes, jackfruits, and the like — that is <s>nirjarā</s> not arising from [natural] fruition. The word 'ca' (and) is for the purpose of conjoining another cause. It will be said, 'and <s>nirjarā</s> through <s>tapas</s> (austerity)'; thus the meaning of the sūtra is construed as 'from that and also from another [cause].' Why is <s>nirjarā</s> mentioned here, when it should be mentioned after <s>saṃvara</s> as in the enumeration? The statement is made here for brevity. For in that arrangement, one would have to repeat 'fruition is experience.'

children.text: § 779. āha abhihito ’nubhavabandhaḥ. idānīṃ pradeśabandho vaktavyaḥ. tasmiṃś ca vaktavye sati ime nirdeṣṭavyāḥ — kiṃ hetavaḥ kadā kutaḥ kiṃ svabhāvāḥ kasmin kiṃ parimāṇaś ceti? tadartham idaṃ krameṇa parigṛhītapraśnāpekṣabhedaṃ sūtraṃ praṇīyate —
children.translated_text: Section 779. One says: the bondage of experience has been stated. Now the bondage of spatial units (<s>pradeśabandha</s>) is to be stated. And in stating that, these things must be specified: what are the causes, when, from where, of what nature, in what [locus], and of what measure? For this purpose, the following sūtra is composed, addressing these questions in sequence —

children.text: nāmapratyayāḥ sarvato yogaviśeṣāt sūkṣmaikakṣetrāvagāhasthitāḥ sarvātmapradeśeṣv anantānantapradeśāḥ ||
children.translated_text: [The spatial units of karma] are named by their causes (<s>nāmapratyayāḥ</s>); [they are taken] from all [existences]; through the particular activity of <s>yoga</s> (mind, speech, body); being subtle, occupying the same space (<s>ekakṣetrāvagāha</s>), and stationary; [they abide] in all spatial units of the soul; [and they consist of] infinitely infinite spatial units.

children.text: § 780. nāmnaḥ pratyayā nāmapratyayāh ‘nāma’ iti sarvāḥ karmaprakṛtayo ’bhidhīyante; ‘sa yathānāma’ iti vacanāt. anena hetubhāva uktaḥ. sarveṣu bhaveṣu sarvataḥ ‘dṛśyante anyato ’pi’ iti tasi kṛte sarvataḥ. anena kālopādānaṃ iti kṛtam. ekaikasya hi jīvasyātikrāntā anantā bhavā āgāminaḥ saṃkhyeyā asaṃkhyeyā anantānantā vā bhavantīti. yogaviśeṣān nimittāt karmabhāvena pudgalā ādīyanta iti nimittaviśeṣanirdeśaḥ kṛto bhavati. ‘sūkṣma’ ādigrahaṇaṃ karmagrahaṇayogyapudgalasvabhāvānuvartanārtham, grahaṇayogyāḥ pudgalāḥ sūkṣmā na sthūlā iti. ‘ekakṣetrāvagāha’ vacanaṃ kṣetrāntaranivṛttyartham. ‘sthitāḥ’ iti vacanaṃ kriyāntaranivṛttyartham, sthitā na gacchanta iti. ‘sarvātmapradeśeṣu’ iti vacanam ādhāranirdeśārthaṃ naikapradeśādiṣu karmapradeśā vartante. kva tarhi? ūrdhvam adhas tiryak ca sarveṣv ātmapradeśeṣu vyāpya sthitā iti. ‘anantānantapradeśa’ vacanaṃ parimāṇāntaravyapohārtham, na saṃkhyeyā na cāsaṃkhyeyā nāpy anantā iti. te khalu pudgalaskandhā abhavyānantaguṇāḥ siddhānantabhāgapramitapradeśā ghanāṅgulasyāsaṃkhyeyabhāgakṣetrāvagāhina ekadvitricatuḥsaṃkhyeyasamayasthitikāḥ pañcavarṇapañcarasa-dvigandha-catuḥsparśasvabhāvā aṣṭavidhakarmaprakṛtiyogyā yogavaśād ātmanātmasāt kriyante. iti pradeśa-bandhaḥ samāsato veditavyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 780. <s>Nāmapratyayāḥ</s> means 'those whose causes are names' — here 'name' refers to all types of <s>karma</s>, because of the statement 'it is according to name.' By this, the causal nature is stated. 'From everywhere' (sarvataḥ) — 'they are seen from elsewhere also' — with the ablative suffix applied, [we get] 'from all [existences].' By this, the specification of time is accomplished. For each soul, past existences are infinite, while future ones are countable, uncountable, or infinitely infinite. [The karmic matter] is taken as karma through the particular activity of <s>yoga</s> — thus the specification of the instrumental cause is stated. The terms 'subtle' and so forth serve to indicate the nature of the material particles (<s>pudgalas</s>) suitable for karmic uptake — the particles suitable for uptake are subtle, not gross. The expression 'occupying the same space' is to exclude other spatial locations. The word 'stationary' is to exclude other activities — they are stationary, not moving. 'In all spatial units of the soul' specifies the locus — the karmic spatial units do not exist in just one or a few spatial units; rather, they pervade all spatial units of the soul — above, below, and across — and remain established. The expression 'infinitely infinite spatial units' is to exclude other measures — they are neither countable, nor uncountable, nor merely infinite. These material aggregates (<s>pudgalaskandhas</s>) are infinitely greater than [the number of] non-liberatable [souls], have spatial units measured as an infinite fraction of liberated [souls], occupy a space that is an uncountable fraction of a cubic <s>aṅgula</s>, have durations of one, two, three, four, or countable time-instants, possess five colors, five tastes, two odors, and four touches by nature, are suitable for the eight types of <s>karma</s>, and are appropriated by the soul through the force of <s>yoga</s>. Thus <s>pradeśabandha</s> (bondage of spatial units) should be understood in brief.

children.text: § 781. āha, bandhapadārthāntaraṃ puṇyapāpopasaṃkhyānaṃ coditaṃ tadbandhe ’ntarbhūtam iti pratyākhyātam. tatredaṃ vaktavyaṃ ko ’tra puṇyabandhaḥ kaḥ pāpabandha iti. tatra puṇyaprakṛtiparigaṇanārtham idam ārabhyate —
children.translated_text: Section 781. One says: another aspect of the category of bondage — the classification of merit (<s>puṇya</s>) and demerit (<s>pāpa</s>) — was raised but was rejected as being included within bondage. Now this must be stated: what constitutes meritorious bondage and what constitutes demeritorious bondage? For the purpose of enumerating the meritorious types, this is commenced —

children.text: sadvedyaśubhāyurnāmagotrāṇi puṇyam ||
children.translated_text: Pleasant feeling-producing (<s>sadvedya</s>), auspicious life-span (<s>śubhāyus</s>), [auspicious] name-determining (<s>nāma</s>), and [auspicious] lineage-determining (<s>gotra</s>) constitute merit (<s>puṇya</s>).

children.text: § 782. śubhaṃ praśastam iti yāvat. taduttaraiḥ pratyekam abhisaṃbadhyate śubham āyuḥ śubhaṃ nāma śubhaṃ gotram iti. śubhāyus tritayaṃ tiryagāyur manuṣyāyur devāyur iti. śubhanāma saptatriṃśad vikalpam. tad yathā — manuṣyagatir devagatiḥ paṃcendriyajāti paṃca śarīrāṇi trīṇy aṅgopāṅgāni samacaturasrasaṃsthānaṃ vajrarṣabhanārācasaṃhananaṃ praśastavarṇarasagandhasparśā manuṣyadevagatyānupūrvyadvayam agurulaghuparaghātocchvāsātapodyotapraśastavihāyogatayas trasabādaraparyāptipratyekaśarīrasthiraśubhasubhagasusvarādeyayaśaḥkīrtayo nirmāṇaṃ tīrthakaranāma ceti. śubham ekam uccairgotraṃ, sadvedyam iti. etā dvācatvāriṃśatprakṛtayaḥ ‘puṇya’ saṃjñāḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 782. 'Śubha' means auspicious or praiseworthy. It connects individually with each subsequent term: auspicious life-span, auspicious name, auspicious lineage. Auspicious life-span is of three kinds: animal life-span, human life-span, and celestial life-span. Auspicious <s>nāma</s> karma is of thirty-seven sub-types, namely: human destiny, celestial destiny, five-sensed birth, five bodies, three types of limbs and minor limbs, symmetrical bodily frame, <s>vajraṛṣabhanārāca</s> (adamantine) bone-joint structure, praiseworthy color, taste, smell, and touch, the two sequential-form karmas of human and celestial destinies, non-heavy-non-light, self-destructive capacity, respiration, radiance, lustre, praiseworthy locomotion, mobile, gross, fully developed, individual body, stable, beautiful, attractive voice, beloved, fame, and glory, the power of transformation (<s>nirmāṇa</s>), and <s>tīrthakaranāma</s> (the name-karma of a ford-maker). Auspicious <s>gotra</s> is one: high lineage (<s>uccairgotra</s>). And pleasant feeling-producing (<s>sadvedya</s>). These forty-two types are designated as 'merit' (<s>puṇya</s>).

children.text: ato ’nyat pāpam ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is other than this is demerit (<s>pāpa</s>).

children.text: § 783. asmat puṇyasaṃjñikarmaprakṛtisamūhād anyat karma ‘pāpam’ ity ucyate. tad dvyaśītividham. tad yathā — jñānāvaraṇasya prakṛtayaḥ paṃca darśanāvaraṇasya nava mohanīyasya ṣaḍviṃśatiḥ paṃcāntarāyasya narakagatitiryaggatī catasro jātayaḥ paṃca saṃsthānāni paṃca saṃhananānyapraśastavarṇarasagandhasparśā narakagatitiryaggatyānupūrvyadvayam upaghātāpraśastavihāyogatisthāvarasūkṣmāparyāptisādhāraṇaśarīrāsthirāśubhadurbhagaduḥsvarānādeyāyaśaḥkīrtayaś ceti nāmakṛtayaś catustriṃśat. asad vedyaṃ narakāyur nīcairgotram iti. evaṃ vyākhyātaḥ saprapañco bandhapadārthaḥ. avadhimanaḥparyayakevalajñānapratyakṣapramāṇagamyas tadupadiṣṭāgamānumeyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 783. Karma other than this collection of types designated as merit is called '<s>pāpa</s>' (demerit). It is of eighty-two kinds, namely: five sub-types of <s>jñānāvaraṇa</s> (knowledge-obscuring), nine of <s>darśanāvaraṇa</s> (perception-obscuring), twenty-six of <s>mohanīya</s> (deluding), five of <s>antarāya</s> (obstructive), hellish destiny, animal destiny, four types of birth, five bodily frames, five bone-joint structures, unpraiseworthy color, taste, smell, and touch, the two sequential-form karmas of hellish and animal destinies, self-harming capacity, unpraiseworthy locomotion, immobile, subtle, undeveloped, common body, unstable, ugly, repulsive voice, disliked, and infamy — these being thirty-four sub-types of <s>nāma</s> karma. [Additionally:] unpleasant feeling-producing (<s>asadvedya</s>), hellish life-span (<s>narakāyus</s>), and low lineage (<s>nīcairgotra</s>). Thus the category of bondage has been explained in detail. It is knowable through <s>avadhi</s> (clairvoyant), <s>manaḥparyaya</s> (mind-reading), and <s>kevala</s> (omniscient) direct cognition (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), as valid means of knowledge, and is inferrable from the scripture taught by those [omniscient beings].

children.text: iti tattvārthavṛttau sarvārthasiddhisaṃjñikāyāṃ aṣṭamo ’dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ || 8 ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the eighth chapter in the <s>Sarvārthasiddhi</s>, the commentary on the <s>Tattvārthasūtra</s>. || 8 ||

children.text: atha navamo ’dhyāyaḥ
children.translated_text: Now begins the ninth chapter.

children.text: § 784. bandhapadārtho nirdiṣṭaḥ. idānīṃ tadantaroddeśabhājaḥ saṃvarasya nirdeśaḥ prāptakāla ity ata idam āha —
children.translated_text: Section 784. The category of bondage has been taught. Now it is time for the exposition of <s>saṃvara</s> (stoppage of karmic influx), which is the subject of the next topic in the enumeration. Therefore he states —

children.text: āsravanirodhaḥ saṃvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: The stoppage of <s>āsrava</s> (karmic influx) is <s>saṃvara</s>.

children.text: § 785. abhinavakarmādānahetur āsravo vyākhyātaḥ. tasya nirodhaḥ saṃvara ity ucyate. sa dvividho bhāvasaṃvaro dravyasaṃvaraś ceti. tatra saṃsāranimittakriyānivṛttir bhāvasaṃvaraḥ. tannirodhe tatpūrvakarmapudgalādānavicchedo dravyasaṃvaraḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 785. <s>Āsrava</s>, the cause of the intake of fresh <s>karma</s>, has been explained. Its stoppage is called <s>saṃvara</s>. It is of two kinds: <s>bhāvasaṃvara</s> (psychic stoppage) and <s>dravyasaṃvara</s> (material stoppage). Of these, the cessation of activities that cause worldly existence (<s>saṃsāra</s>) is <s>bhāvasaṃvara</s>. Upon that cessation, the cutting off of the intake of karmic material particles that was caused by those [activities] is <s>dravyasaṃvara</s>.

children.text: § 786. idaṃ vicāryate — kasmin guṇasthāne kasya saṃvara iti? atra ucyate — mithyādarśanakarmodayavaśīkṛta ātmā mithyādṛṣṭiḥ. tatra mithyādarśanaprādhānyena yatkarma āsravati tannirodhāc cheṣe sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭyādau tatsaṃvaro bhavati. kiṃ punas tat? mithyātvanapuṃsakavedanarakāyur narakagatyekadvitricaturindriyajātihuṇḍasaṃsthānāsaṃprāptāsṛpāṭikāsaṃhanananarakagatiprāyogyānupūrvyātapasthāvarasūkṣmāparyāptakasādhāraṇaśarīrasaṃjñakaṣoḍaśaprakṛtilakṣaṇam.
children.translated_text: Section 786. This is now examined: at which guṇasthāna (spiritual stage) does stoppage (saṃvara) occur for whom? Here it is stated: the soul dominated by the rise of wrong-faith karma is a mithyādṛṣṭi (one of wrong faith). There, whatever karma flows in predominantly due to wrong faith — from the cessation of that, in the remaining stages beginning with sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi (one in declining right faith), its stoppage occurs. What then is that? It is characterized by sixteen types (prakṛtis), namely: mithyātva (wrong faith), napuṃsakaveda (neuter gender), narakāyus (hellish life-span), narakagati (hellish destiny), one-sensed, two-sensed, three-sensed, and four-sensed birth-types, huṇḍa (hunchback) bodily frame, disproportionate body, asṛpāṭikā (riveted) bone-joint structure, the sequential-form karma of hellish destiny, heat (ātapa), immobile (sthāvara), subtle (sūkṣma), undeveloped (aparyāptaka), and common body (sādhāraṇaśarīra).

children.text: § 787. asaṃyamas trividhaḥ; anantānubandhyapratyākhyānapratyākhyānodayavikalpāt. tatpratyayasya karmaṇas tadabhāve saṃvaro ’vaseyaḥ. tad yathā — nidrānidrāpracalāpracalāstyānagṛddhyanantānubandhikrodhamānamāyālobhastrīvedatiryagāyustiryaggaticatuḥ-saṃsthānacatuḥsaṃhananatiryaggatiprāyogyānupūrvyodyotāpraśastavihāyogatidurbhagaduḥsvarānādeyanīcairgotrasaṃjñikānāṃ pañcaviṃśatiprakṛtīnām anantānubandhikaṣāyodayakṛtāsaṃyamapradhānāsravāṇām ekendriyādayaḥ sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭyantā bandhakāḥ. tadabhāve tāsām uttaratra saṃvaraḥ. apratyākhyānāvaraṇakrodhamānamāyālobhamanuṣyāyurmanuṣyagatyaudārikaśarīratadaṅgopāṅgavajrarṣabhanārācasaṃhananamanuṣyagatiprāyogyānupūrvyanāmnā daśānāṃ prakṛtīnām apratyākhyānakaṣāyodayakṛtāsaṃyamahetukānām ekendriyādayo ’saṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭyantā bandhakāḥ. tadabhāvād ūrdhvaṃ tāsāṃ saṃvaraḥ. samyaṅmithyātvaguṇenāyur na badhyate. pratyākhyānāvaraṇakrodhamānamāyālobhānāṃ catasṛṇāṃ prakṛtīnāṃ pratyākhyānakaṣāyodayakāraṇāsaṃyamāsravāṇām ekendriyaprabhṛtayaḥ saṃyatāsaṃyatāvasānā bandhakāḥ. tadabhāvād upariṣṭāt tāsāṃ saṃvaraḥ. pramādopanītasya tadabhāve nirodhaḥ. pramādenopanītasya karmaṇaḥ pramattasaṃyatād ūrdhvaṃ tadabhāvān nirodhaḥ pratyetavyaḥ. kiṃ punas tat. asadvedyāratiśokāsthirāśubhāyaśaḥkīrtivikalpam. devāyurbandhārambhasya pramāda eva hetur apramādo ’pi tat pratyāsannaḥ. tadūrdhvaṃ tasya saṃvaraḥ. kaṣāya evāsravo yasya karmaṇo na pramādādiḥ tasya tannirodhe nirāso ’vaseyaḥ. sa ca kaṣāyaḥ pramādādivirahitas tīvramadhyamajaghanyabhāvena triṣu guṇasthāneṣu vyavasthitaḥ. tatrāpūrvakaraṇasyādau saṃkhyeyabhāge dve karmaprakṛtī nidrāpracale badhyete. tata ūrdhvaṃ saṃkhyeyabhāge triṃśat prakṛtayo devagatipañcendriyajātivaikriyikāhārakataijasakārmaṇaśarīrasamacaturasrasaṃsthānavaikriyikāhārakaśarīrāṃgopāṃgavarṇagandharasasparśadevagatiprāyogyānupūrvyāgurulaghūpaghātaparaghātocchvāsapraśastavihāyogatitrasabādaraparyāptapratyekaśarīrasthiraśubhasubhagasusvarādeyanirmāṇatīrthakarākhyā badhyante. tasyaiva caramasamaye catasraḥ prakṛtayo hāsyaratibhayajugupsāsaṃjñā bandham upayānti. tā etās tīvrakaṣāyāsravās tadabhāvān nirddiṣṭād bhāgād ūrdhvaṃ saṃvriyante. anivṛttibādarasāṃparāyasyādisamayād ārabhya saṃkhyeyeṣu bhāgeṣu puṃvedakrodhasaṃjvalanau badhyete. tata ūrdhvaṃ śeṣeṣu saṃkhyeyeṣu bhāgeṣu mānasaṃjvalanamāyāsaṃjvalanau bandham upagacchataḥ. tasyaiva caramasamaye lobhasaṃjvalano bandham eti. tā etāḥ prakṛtayo madhyamakaṣāyāsravās tadabhāve nirdiṣṭasya bhāgasyopariṣṭāt saṃvaram āpnuvanti. pañcānāṃ jñānāvaraṇānāṃ caturṇāṃ darśanāvaraṇānāṃ yaśaḥkīrter uccairgotrasya pañcānām antarāyāṇāṃ ca mandakaṣāyāsravāṇāṃ sūkṣmasāṃparāyo bandhakaḥ. tadabhāvād uttararatra teṣāṃ saṃvaraḥ. kevalenaiva yogena sadvedyasopaśāntakaṣāyakṣīṇakaṣāyasayogānāṃ bandho bhavati. tadabhāvād ayogakevalinas tasya saṃvaro bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 787. Non-restraint (asaṃyama) is threefold, according to the distinction of the rise of anantānubandhin (infinitely binding), apratyākhyāna (non-renunciation-type), and pratyākhyāna (renunciation-type) [passions]. The stoppage of the karma caused by those [passions] should be understood as occurring in their absence. That is as follows: the twenty-five types (prakṛtis) — namely, nidrā (sleep), nidrānidrā (deep sleep), pracalā (drowsiness), pracalāpracalā (intense drowsiness), styānagṛddhi (somnambulism), anantānubandhi anger, pride, deceit, and greed, feminine gender (strīveda), animal life-span (tiryagāyus), animal destiny (tiryaggati), four bodily frames, four bone-joint structures, the sequential-form karma of animal destiny, radiance (udyota), unpraiseworthy locomotion (apraśastavihāyogati), misfortune (durbhaga), repulsive voice (duḥsvara), unattractiveness (anādeya), low lineage (nīcairgotra) — designated as having influx predominantly caused by the rise of anantānubandhin passions, are bound by beings from one-sensed onward up to sāsādanasamyagdṛṣṭi. In their absence, the stoppage of those [types] occurs in the subsequent stages. The ten types named apratyākhyānāvaraṇa anger, pride, deceit, and greed, human life-span (manuṣyāyus), human destiny (manuṣyagati), gross physical body (audārikaśarīra), its limbs and minor limbs, vajraṛṣabhanārāca (adamantine) bone-joint structure, and the sequential-form karma of human destiny — whose influx of non-restraint is caused by the rise of apratyākhyāna passions, are bound by beings from one-sensed onward up to asaṃyatasamyagdṛṣṭi (the unrestrained right-believer). From their absence upward, the stoppage of those [types] occurs. Through the quality of mixed right-and-wrong faith (samyaṅmithyātva), life-span karma is not bound. The four types of pratyākhyānāvaraṇa anger, pride, deceit, and greed — whose influx of non-restraint is caused by the rise of pratyākhyāna passions — are bound by beings from one-sensed onward up to saṃyatāsaṃyata (the partially restrained). From their absence upward, the stoppage of those [types] occurs. That which is brought about by negligence (pramāda) — its cessation occurs in the absence of that. The karma brought about by negligence should be understood as ceasing above the negligent restrained (pramattasaṃyata) stage, due to the absence of that [negligence]. What then is that? It consists of the sub-varieties of unpleasant feeling-producing (asadvedya), displeasure (arati), sorrow (śoka), instability (asthira), inauspiciousness (aśubha), infamy (ayaśaḥkīrti). Negligence alone is the cause of commencing the bondage of celestial life-span (devāyus), though non-negligence is also close to that [stage]. Above that, its stoppage occurs. For the karma whose influx is caused solely by passions (kaṣāya) and not by negligence and the rest, the cessation should be understood as occurring upon the cessation of those [passions]. And that passion, devoid of negligence and the rest, is established in three spiritual stages in its intense, medium, and mild forms. There, at the beginning of the apūrvakaraṇa (unprecedented process) stage, during a countable fraction [of time], two karmic types — nidrā (sleep) and pracalā (drowsiness) — are bound. Above that, during a countable fraction, thirty types are bound, namely: celestial destiny (devagati), five-sensed birth, transformative body (vaikriyika), assimilative body (āhāraka), luminous body (taijasa), karmic body (kārmaṇa), symmetrical bodily frame (samacaturasra), the limbs and minor limbs of transformative and assimilative bodies, color (varṇa), smell (gandha), taste (rasa), touch (sparśa), the sequential-form karma of celestial destiny, non-heavy-non-light (agurulaghu), self-destructive capacity (upaghāta), other-destructive capacity (paraghāta), respiration (ucchvāsa), praiseworthy locomotion (praśastavihāyogati), mobile (trasa), gross (bādara), fully developed (paryāpta), individual body (pratyekaśarīra), stable (sthira), beautiful (śubha), fortunate (subhaga), attractive voice (susvara), attractiveness (ādeya), power of transformation (nirmāṇa), and the name-karma of a ford-maker (tīrthakaranāma). At the last moment of that very [stage], four types — laughter (hāsya), pleasure (rati), fear (bhaya), and disgust (jugupsā) — enter into bondage. These, having influx caused by intense passions, are stopped above the stated fraction [of time] due to the absence of those [passions]. From the first moment of the anivṛttibādarasāṃparāya (non-retreating gross-passion) stage, during countable fractions, masculine gender (puṃveda) and anger of the saṃjvalana (blazing) type are bound. Above that, during the remaining countable fractions, pride of the saṃjvalana type and deceit of the saṃjvalana type enter into bondage. At the last moment of that very [stage], greed of the saṃjvalana type enters into bondage. These types, having influx caused by medium passions, attain stoppage above the stated fraction due to the absence of those [passions]. The five sub-types of jñānāvaraṇa (knowledge-obscuring), four of darśanāvaraṇa (perception-obscuring), fame (yaśaḥkīrti), high lineage (uccairgotra), and five antarāyas (obstructive karmas) — having influx caused by mild passions — are bound by sūkṣmasāṃparāya (one at the stage of subtle mixed passions). In their absence, the stoppage of those occurs at the subsequent stage. Through activity (yoga) alone, the bondage of pleasant feeling-producing (sadvedya) occurs for the upaśāntakaṣāya (one with subsided passions), kṣīṇakaṣāya (one with destroyed passions), and the omniscient with activity (sayogakevalin). In the absence of that [activity], its stoppage occurs for the omniscient without activity (ayogakevalin).

children.text: § 788. uktaḥ saṃvaras taddhetupratipādanārtham āha —
children.translated_text: Section 788. Saṃvara (stoppage) has been stated. In order to explain its causes, he says —

children.text: sa guptisamitidharmānuprekṣāpariṣahajayacāritraiḥ ||
children.translated_text: That [stoppage is achieved] through guptis (guards), samitis (carefulness), dharmas (virtues), anuprekṣās (contemplations), pariṣahajaya (conquest of hardships), and cāritra (right conduct). ||

children.text: § 789. yataḥ saṃsārakāraṇād ātmano gopanaṃ bhavati sā guptiḥ. prāṇipīḍāparihārārthaṃ samyagayanaṃ samitiḥ. iṣṭe sthāne dhatte iti dharmaḥ. śarīrādīnāṃ svabhāvānucintanam anuprekṣā. kṣudādivedanotpattau karmanirjarārthaṃ sahanaṃ pariṣahaḥ. pariṣahasya jayaḥ pariṣahajayaḥ. cāritraśabda ādisūtre vyākhyātārthaḥ. eteṣāṃ guptyādīnāṃ saṃvaraṇakriyāyāḥ sādhakatamatvād karaṇanirdeśaḥ. saṃvaro ’dhikṛto ’pi ‘sa’ iti tacchabdena parāmṛśyate guptyādibhiḥ sākṣāt saṃbandhanārthaḥ. kiṃ prayojanam? avadhāraṇārtham. sa eṣa saṃvaro guptyādibhir eva nānyenopāyeneti. tena tīrthābhiṣekadīkṣāśīrṣopahāradevatārādhananādayo nivartitā bhavanti; rāgadveṣamohopāttasya karmaṇo ’nyathā nivṛttyabhāvāt.
children.translated_text: Section 789. Gupti (guarding) is that by which the soul is protected from the causes of worldly existence. Samiti (carefulness) is the proper movement for the purpose of avoiding harm to living beings. Dharma (virtue) is that which holds one in the desired state. Anuprekṣā (contemplation) is the reflection on the true nature of the body and so forth. Pariṣaha (hardship) is the endurance, for the purpose of shedding karma, when sensations of hunger and the like arise. Pariṣahajaya is the conquest of hardship. The word cāritra (right conduct) has its meaning explained in the initial sūtra. The instrumental case is used for guptis and the rest because they are the most effective means of accomplishing the act of stoppage. Although saṃvara is the topic under discussion, it is referred back to by the pronoun 'sa' (that) for the purpose of directly connecting it with guptis and the rest. What is the purpose? For the purpose of restriction — that this very saṃvara is [achieved] through guptis and the rest alone, and by no other means. Thereby, [practices such as] bathing in sacred fords, initiation, tonsure, offering to deities, worshiping deities through chanting, and the like are excluded, since karma acquired through attachment, aversion, and delusion cannot be stopped otherwise.

children.text: § 790. saṃvaranirjarāhetuviśeṣapratipādanārtham āha —
children.translated_text: Section 790. In order to explain the specific causes of saṃvara (stoppage) and nirjarā (shedding), he says —

children.text: tapasā nirjarā ca ||
children.translated_text: And nirjarā (shedding of karma) [is achieved] through tapas (austerity). ||

children.text: § 791. tapo dharme ’ntarbhūtam api pṛthagucyate ubhayasādhanatvakhyāpanārthaṃ saṃvaraṃ prati prādhānyapratipādanārthaṃ ca. nanu ca tapo ’bhudayāṃgam iṣtaṃ devendrādisthānaprāptihetutvābhyupagamāt, tat kathaṃ nirjarāṃgaṃ syād iti? naiṣa doṣaḥ; ekasyānekakāryadarśanād agnivat. yathāgnir eko ’pi vikledanabhasmāṃgārādiprayojana upalabhyate tathā tapo ’bhudayakarmakṣayahetur ity atra ko virodhaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 791. Although tapas (austerity) is included within dharma (virtue), it is stated separately for the purpose of declaring that it is a means to both [stoppage and shedding], and for establishing its pre-eminence with respect to saṃvara. But is not tapas accepted as a component of worldly prosperity, since it is acknowledged as a cause of attaining positions such as Devendra (lord of gods) and the like? How then can it be a component of nirjarā? This is no defect, because a single thing is seen to have multiple effects, like fire. Just as fire, though one, is observed to serve purposes of evaporation, turning to ash, making embers, and the like, what contradiction is there in tapas being a cause of both worldly prosperity and the destruction of karma?

children.text: § 792. saṃvarahetuṣv ādāv uddiṣṭāyā gupteḥ svarūpapratipattyartham āha —
children.translated_text: Section 792. In order to ascertain the nature of gupti (guarding), which was mentioned first among the causes of saṃvara, he says —

children.text: samyagyoganigraho guptiḥ ||
children.translated_text: The proper restraint of activity (yoga) is gupti (guarding). ||

children.text: § 793. yogo vyākhyātaḥ ‘kāyavāṅmanaḥkarma yogaḥ’ ity atra. tasya svecchāpravṛttinivartanaṃ nigrahaḥ. viṣayasukhābhilāṣārthapravṛttiniṣedhārthaṃ samyagviśeṣaṇam. tasmāt samyagviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭāt saṃkleśāprādurbhāvaparātkāyādiyoganirodhe sati tannimittaṃ karma nāsravatīti saṃvaraprasiddhir avagantavyā. sā tritayī kāyaguptir vāgguptir manoguptir iti.
children.translated_text: Section 793. Yoga (activity) has been explained in the passage 'activity of body, speech, and mind is yoga.' Its restraint (nigraha) is the prevention of its impulsive operation. The qualifier 'samyak' (proper) is for the purpose of prohibiting activity directed toward the desire for sensual pleasure. Therefore, when the restraint of bodily and other activities — qualified by the qualifier 'proper' and characterized by the non-arising of affliction (saṃkleśa) — is accomplished, the karma caused by that [activity] does not flow in; thus the establishment of saṃvara should be understood. That [guarding] is threefold: guarding of body (kāyagupti), guarding of speech (vāggupti), and guarding of mind (manogupti).

children.text: § 794. tatrāśaktasya muner niravadyapravṛttikhyāpanārtham āha —
children.translated_text: Section 794. In order to declare the blameless conduct of a monk who is unable [to completely restrain activity], he says —

children.text: īryābhāṣaiṣaṇādānanikṣepotsargāḥ samitayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Walking (īryā), speaking (bhāṣā), seeking alms (eṣaṇā), picking up and putting down (ādānanikṣepa), and excretion (utsarga) are the samitis (carefulness). ||

children.text: § 795. ‘samyag’ ity anuvartate. teneryādayo viśeṣyante. samyagīryā samyagbhāṣā samyageṣaṇā samyagādānanikṣepau samyagutsarga iti. sā etāḥ pañca samitayo viditajīvasthānādividher muneḥ prāṇipīḍāparihārābhyupāyā veditavyāḥ. tathā pravartamānsyāsaṃyamapariṇāmanimittakarmāsravāt saṃvaro bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 795. The word 'samyak' (proper) continues [from the previous sūtra]; thereby walking and the rest are qualified. [They are:] proper walking, proper speaking, proper seeking of alms, proper picking up and putting down, and proper excretion. These five samitis should be understood as the means of avoiding harm to living beings for a monk who knows the rules regarding the abodes of life-forms and the like. When one thus conducts oneself, saṃvara (stoppage) occurs from the karmic influx caused by the disposition of non-restraint.

children.text: § 796. tṛitīyasya saṃvarahetor dharmasya bhedapratipattyartham āha —
children.translated_text: Section 796. In order to ascertain the divisions of dharma (virtue), the third cause of saṃvara, he says —

children.text: uttamakṣamāmārdavārjavasaucasatyasaṃyamatapastyāgākiṃcanyabrahmacaryāṇi dharmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Supreme forbearance (kṣamā), humility (mārdava), straightforwardness (ārjava), purity (śauca), truthfulness (satya), restraint (saṃyama), austerity (tapas), renunciation (tyāga), non-possessiveness (ākiṃcanya), and celibacy (brahmacarya) constitute dharma (virtue). ||

children.text: § 797. kim artham idam ucyate? ādyaṃ pravṛttinigrahārtham, tatrāsamarthānāṃ pravṛttyupāyadarśanārtham dvitīyam. idaṃ punar daśāvidhadharmākhyānaṃ samitiṣu pravartamānasya pramādaparihārārthaṃ veditavyam. śarīrasthitihetumārgaṇārthaṃ parakulāny upagacchato bhikṣor duṣṭajanākrośaprahasanāvajñātāḍanaśarīravyāpādanādīnāṃ saṃnidhāne kāluṣyānupattiḥ kṣamā. jātyādimadāveśād abhimānābhāvo mārdavaṃ mānanirharaṇam. yogasyāvarkratā ārjavam. prakarśaprāptalobhān nivṛttiḥ śaucam. satsu praśasteṣu janeṣu sādhu vacanaṃ satyam ity ucyate. nanu caitad bhāṣāsamitāv antarbhavati? naiṣa doṣaḥ; samitau pravartamāno muniḥ sādhuṣv asādhuṣu ca bhāṣāvyavahāraṃ kurvan hitaṃ mitaṃ ca brūyāt anyathā rāgād anarthadaṇḍadoṣaḥ syād iti vāksamitir ity arthaḥ. iha punaḥ saṃtaḥ pravrajitās tadbhaktā vā teṣu sādhu satyaṃ jñānacāritraśikṣaṇādiṣu bahvapi kartavyam ity anujñāyate dharmopabṛṃhaṇārtham. samitiṣu vartamānasya prāṇīndriya -parihāras saṃyamaḥ. karmakṣayārthaṃ tapyata iti tapaḥ. taduttrartra vakṣyamāṇaṃ dvādaśavikalpam avaseyam. saṃyatasya yogyaṃ jñānādidānaṃ tyāgaḥ. upātteṣv api śarīrādiṣu saṃskārāpohāya mamedam ity abhisandhinivṛttir ākiṃcanyam. nāsya kiṃcanāstīty akiṃcanaḥ tasya bhāvaḥ karma vā ākiṃcanyam. anubhūtāṅganāsmaraṇakathāśravaṇastrīsaṃsaktaśayanāsanādivarjanād brahmacaryaṃ paripūrṇam avatiṣṭhate. svatantravṛttinirvṛttyartho vā gurukulavāso brahmacaryam. dṛṣṭaprayojanaparivarjanārtham uttamaviśeṣaṇam. tāny evaṃ bhāvyamānāni dharmavyapadeśabhāñjisvaguṇapraptipakṣadoṣasadbhāvanāpraṇihitāni saṃvarakāraṇāni bhavanti.
children.translated_text: Section 797. For what purpose is this stated? The first [teaching on guptis] was for the purpose of restraining activity; the second [on samitis], for showing the means of activity for those unable [to fully restrain]. This declaration of the tenfold dharma should be understood as being for the purpose of avoiding negligence while engaged in the samitis. Kṣamā (forbearance) is the non-arising of agitation when, while a mendicant approaches other households for the purpose of seeking what sustains the body, there occur abuse, mockery, contempt, beating, bodily harm, and the like from wicked people. Mārdava (humility) is the absence of pride arising from intoxication of birth and the like — it is the removal of arrogance. Ārjava (straightforwardness) is the non-crookedness of activity. Śauca (purity) is the cessation of greed that has reached an extreme degree. Satya (truthfulness) is said to be wholesome speech among good and praiseworthy people. But does this not fall within the carefulness of speech (bhāṣāsamiti)? This is no defect; a monk engaged in the carefulness [of speech], while conducting verbal transactions with both the good and the bad, should speak what is beneficial and measured — otherwise, from attachment, the fault of purposeless speech (anarthadaṇḍa) would arise. This is the meaning of speech-carefulness. But here, among the virtuous — whether renouncers or their devotees — even abundant wholesome and truthful speech regarding instruction in knowledge, conduct, and the like is permitted, for the purpose of strengthening dharma. Saṃyama (restraint) is the avoidance of harming living beings and their senses while engaged in the samitis. Tapas (austerity) is that by which one burns for the destruction of karma; it should be understood as being of twelve kinds, which will be stated later. Tyāga (renunciation) is the giving of knowledge and the like that is fitting for a restrained person. Ākiṃcanya (non-possessiveness) is the cessation of the notion 'this is mine' — the removal of attachment — even with respect to the body and other things that have been adopted. One who has nothing is akiṃcana; its state or the practice thereof is ākiṃcanya. Brahmacarya (celibacy) is fulfilled completely through avoiding the recollection of women previously enjoyed, listening to stories [about women], sitting and sleeping in places associated with women, and the like. Alternatively, brahmacarya is residence in the teacher's household for the purpose of sustaining one's independent life. The qualifier 'uttama' (supreme) is for the purpose of excluding [practices] with visible [worldly] purposes. These [virtues], when cultivated in this manner, become causes of saṃvara when they bear the designation of dharma, are oriented toward the attainment of one's own qualities, are [accompanied by] the presence of defects on the opposing side, and are directed without [selfish] purpose.

children.text: § 798. āha, krodhādyanutpattiḥ kṣamādiviśeṣapratyanīkālambanād ity uktam. tatra kasmāt kṣamādīn ayam avalambate nānyathā pravartata ity ucyate. yasmāt taptāyaḥpiṇḍavatkṣamādipariṇatenātmahitaiṣiṇā kartavyāḥ —
children.translated_text: Section 798. One says: it has been stated that the non-arising of anger and the like occurs through relying on the counteracting objects such as forbearance and the like. In that case, why does one take recourse to forbearance and the like rather than act otherwise? It is stated: because, like a heated iron ball, the one who seeks one's own welfare, transformed by forbearance and the like, should practice —

children.text: anityāśaraṇasaṃsāraikatvānyatvāśucyāsravasaṃvaranirjarālokabodhidurlabhadharmasvākhyātatvānucintanam anuprekṣāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Contemplation (anucintana) of impermanence (anitya), helplessness (aśaraṇa), transmigration (saṃsāra), aloneness (ekatva), separateness (anyatva), impurity (aśuci), influx (āsrava), stoppage (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), the world (loka), the difficulty of attaining enlightenment (bodhidurlabha), and the well-proclaimed nature of dharma (dharmasvākhyātatva) — these are the anuprekṣās (contemplations). ||

children.text: § 799. imāni śarīrendriyaviṣayopabhogadravyāṇi samudayarūpāṇi jalabudbudvadanavasthitasvabhāvāni garbhādiṣv avasthāviśeṣeṣu sadupalabhyamānasaṃyogaviparyayāṇi, mohād atrājño nityatāṃ manyate. na kiṃcit saṃsāre samuditaṃ dhruvam asti ātmano jñānadarśanopayogasvabhāvād anyad iti cintanam anityatānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya bhavyasya cintayatas teṣv abhiṣv aṅgābhāvād bhuktojjhitagandhamālyādiṣv iva viyogakāle ’pi vinipāto notpadyate.
children.translated_text: Section 799. These objects — body, senses, enjoyments of sense-objects, and material things — are composite in nature, unstable by nature like water-bubbles, and are observed to undergo conjunction and disjunction in the various stages of existence such as the embryo and the like. Due to delusion, the ignorant person considers them permanent. The contemplation that nothing in saṃsāra (worldly existence), when assembled, is permanent — apart from the soul's own nature characterized by knowledge and perception (jñānadarśanopayoga) — is the contemplation of impermanence (anityatānuprekṣā). For indeed, when a worthy soul thus contemplates, since there is no attachment to those [objects], just as with discarded garlands, flowers, and the like that have been used and abandoned, even at the time of separation, no downfall arises.

children.text: § 800. yathā — mṛgaśāvasyaikānte balavatā kṣudhitenāmiṣaiṣiṇā vyāghreṇābhibhūtasya na kiṃcic charaṇam asti, tathā janmajarāmṛtyuvyādhiprabhṛtivyasanamadhye paribhramato jantoḥ śaraṇaṃ na vidyate. paripuṣtam api śarīraṃ bhojanaṃ prati sahāyībhavati na vyasanopanipāte. yatnena saṃcitā arthā api na bhavāntaram anugacchanti. saṃvibhaktasukhaduḥkhāḥ suhṛdo ’pi na maraṇakāle paritrāyante. bāndhavāḥ samuditāś ca rujā parītaṃ na paripālayanti. asti cet sucarito dharmo vyasanamahārṇave taraṇopāyayo bhavati. mṛtyunā nīyamānasya sahasranayanādayo ’pi na śaraṇam. tasmād bhavavyasanasaṃkaṭe dharma eva śaraṇam. suhṛdartho ’py anapāyī, nānyakiṃcic charaṇam iti bhāvanā aśaraṇānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asyādhyavasyato nityam aśaraṇo ’smīti bhṛśam udvignasya sāṃsārikeṣu bhāveṣu mamatvavigamo bhavati. bhagavadarhatsarvajñapraṇīta eva mārge prayatno bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 800. Just as a deer fawn, overpowered in a solitary place by a powerful, hungry tiger seeking meat, has no refuge whatsoever, so too for a creature revolving amidst calamities such as birth, old age, death, and disease, no refuge is found. Even a well-nourished body serves as an ally only with respect to food, not when calamity strikes. Wealth accumulated with effort does not follow one to the next existence. Friends who have shared happiness and sorrow do not save one at the time of death. Relatives gathered together do not protect one when afflicted by illness. If, however, there is well-practiced <s>dharma</s>, it becomes the means of crossing the great ocean of calamity. Even <s>Sahasranayana</s> (Indra, the thousand-eyed) and others are no refuge for one being led away by death. Therefore, in the peril of worldly calamity, <s>dharma</s> alone is the refuge — a friend whose benefit never perishes — nothing else is a refuge: this contemplation is the <s>aśaraṇānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on helplessness). For when one thus constantly reflects 'I am eternally without refuge,' being greatly distressed, attachment (<s>mamatva</s>) toward worldly things ceases. Effort is directed solely toward the path taught by the blessed, omniscient <s>Arhat</s>.

children.text: § 801. karmavipākavaśād ātmano bhavāntarāvāptiḥ saṃsāraḥ. sa purastāt pañcavidhaparivartanarūpeṇa vyākhyātaḥ. tasminn anekayonikulakoṭibahuśatasahasrasaṃkaṭe saṃsāre paribhraman jīvaḥ karmayantrapreritaḥ pitā bhūtvā bhrātā putraḥ pautraś ca bhavati. mātā bhūtvā bhaginī bhāryā duhitā ca bhavati. svāmī bhūtvā dāso bhavati. dāso bhūtvā svāmy api bhavati. naṭa iva raṅge. athavā kiṃ bahunā, svayam ātmanaḥ putro bhavatīty evam ādi saṃsārasvabhāvacintanaṃ saṃsārānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya bhāvayataḥ saṃsāraduḥkhabhayād udvignasya tato nirvedo bhavati. nirviṇṇaś ca saṃsāragrahāṇāya prayatate.
children.translated_text: Section 801. The attainment of another existence by the soul due to the power of karmic fruition is <s>saṃsāra</s>. It has been previously explained in the form of fivefold revolution. In that <s>saṃsāra</s>, perilous with many hundreds of thousands of crores of birth-species and families, the soul, driven by the machinery of <s>karma</s>, having been a father becomes a brother, a son, and a grandson; having been a mother becomes a sister, a wife, and a daughter; having been a master becomes a slave; having been a slave becomes a master — like an actor on a stage. Or, to put it briefly, one becomes one's own son — such contemplation of the nature of <s>saṃsāra</s> is the <s>saṃsārānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on the cycle of rebirth). For when one thus reflects, being distressed by fear of the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>, dispassion arises toward it. And being dispassionate, one strives to cross over from the clutches of <s>saṃsāra</s>.

children.text: § 802. janmajarāmaraṇāvṛttimahāduḥkhānubhavanaṃ prati eka evāhaṃ na kaścin me svaḥ paro vā vidyate. eka eva jāye ’ham. eka eva mriye. na me kaścit svajanaḥ parajano vā vyādhijarāmaraṇādīni duḥkhāny apaharati. bandhumitrāṇi smaśānaṃ nātivartante. dharma eva me sahāyaḥ sadā anapāyīti cintanam ekatvānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya bhāvayataḥ svajaneṣu prītyanubandho na bhavati. parajaneṣu ca dveṣānubandho nopajāyate. tato niḥsaṅgatām abhyupagato mokṣāyaiva ghaṭate.
children.translated_text: Section 802. With regard to experiencing the great suffering of the cycle of birth, old age, death, and recurrence — I alone [face it]; there is no one, whether my own or another's, [who can help]. I alone am born. I alone die. No kinsman or stranger removes from me the sufferings of disease, old age, death, and the like. Relatives and friends do not pass beyond the cremation ground. <s>Dharma</s> alone is my companion, ever unfailing — such contemplation is the <s>ekatvānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on solitude). For when one thus reflects, attachment toward one's own people does not arise, and aversion toward others does not develop. Thereupon, having embraced detachment, one devotes oneself solely to <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).

children.text: § 803. śarīrād anyatvacintanam anyatvānuprekṣā. tad yathā — bandhaṃ pratyekatve saty api lakṣaṇabhedād anyo ’ham aindriyakaṃ śarīram atīndriyo ’ham ajñaṃ śarīraṃ jño ’ham anityaṃ śarīraṃ nityo ’ham ādy antavaccharīram anādyananto ’ham. bahuni me śarīraśatasahasrāṇy atītāni saṃsāre paribhramataḥ. sa evāham anyas tebhya ity evaṃ me kim aṅga, punarbāhyebhyaḥ parigrahebhyaḥ ity evaṃ hy asya manaḥ samādadhānasya śarīrādiṣu sprhā notpadyate. tatas tattvajñānabhāvanāpūrvake vairāgyaprakarṣe sati ātyantikasya mokṣasukhasyāvāptir bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 803. The contemplation of the soul's otherness from the body is the <s>anyatvānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on separateness). It is as follows: even though there is oneness with respect to bondage, due to difference in defining characteristics, I am other [than the body] — the body is sensory, I am supersensory; the body is unknowing, I am knowing; the body is impermanent, I am permanent; the body has a beginning and an end, I am without beginning and without end. Many hundreds of thousands of bodies have passed as I have wandered in <s>saṃsāra</s>. I am the same [soul], yet different from those [bodies] — if this is so regarding my own limbs, how much more so regarding external possessions! For when one thus concentrates the mind, craving for the body and the like does not arise. Then, when supreme dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) arises, preceded by the cultivation of knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), the attainment of absolute liberation-bliss occurs.

children.text: § 804. śarīram idam atyantāśuciyoni śukraśonitāśucisaṃvardhitam avaskaravadaśucibhājanaṃ tvaṅmātrapracchāditam atipūtirasaniṣyandisrotobilam aṅgāravadātmabhāvam āśritam apy āśvevāpādayati. snānānulepanadhūpapragharṣavāsamālyādibhir api na śakyam aśucitvam apahartum asya. samyagdarśanādi punarbhāvyamānaṃ jīvasyātyantikīṃ śuddhim āvirbhāvayatīti tattvato bhāvanam aśucitavānuprekṣā. evam hy asya saṃsmarataḥ śarīranirvedo bhavati. nirviṇṇaś ca janmodadhitaraṇāya cittaṃ samādhatte.
children.translated_text: Section 804. This body is born from an utterly impure source, nourished by the impure elements of semen and blood, a vessel of impurity like a cesspit, covered only by skin, an abode of extremely foul-smelling streams oozing from its orifices — though the soul has resorted to [this body] as its state of being, like a [glowing] ember, it quickly brings about [revulsion]. Its impurity cannot be removed even by bathing, anointing, incense, scrubbing, garments, garlands, and the like. Right faith and its accompaniments, when contemplated, manifest the ultimate purity of the soul — this is the genuine contemplation of <s>aśucitavānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on impurity). For when one thus reflects, disgust with the body arises. And being disgusted, one concentrates the mind on crossing the ocean of birth.

children.text: § 805. āsravasaṃvaranirjarāḥ pūrvoktā api ihopanyasyante tadgataguṇadoṣabhāvanārtham. tad yathā — āsravā ihāmutrāpāyayuktā mahānadīsrotovegatīkṣṇā indriyakaṣāyā vratādayaḥ.

tatrendriyāṇi tāvat sparśanādīni vanagajavāyasapannagapataṅgahariṇādīn vyavasanārṇavam avagāhayanti tathā kaṣādayo ’pīha vadhabandhāpayaśaḥparikleśādīn janayanti. amutra ca nānāgatiṣu bahuvidhaduḥkhaprajvalitāsu paribhramayantīty evam āsravadoṣānucintanam āsravānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya cintayataḥ kṣamādiṣu śreyas tv abuddhir na pracyavate. sarva ete āsravadoṣāḥ kūrmavatsaṃvṛtātmano na bhavanti.
children.translated_text: Among these, first, the senses — touch and the rest — plunge [beings] like wild elephants, crows, serpents, moths, and deer into the ocean of ruin. Likewise, the passions and the rest generate in this world killing, imprisonment, infamy, affliction, and so forth, and in the next world cause [beings] to revolve through various destinies blazing with manifold sufferings — such contemplation of the faults of influx is the <s>āsravānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on influx). For when one thus reflects, the understanding of what is beneficial, directed toward forbearance and the like, does not waver. All these faults of influx do not arise for one who has withdrawn into himself like a tortoise.

Section 805. <s>Āsrava</s> (influx), <s>saṃvara</s> (stoppage), and <s>nirjarā</s> (shedding), though previously stated, are presented here again for the purpose of contemplating their respective merits and faults. As follows: the <s>āsravas</s>, coupled with harm in this world and the next, fierce as the current of a great river, are the senses and passions (<s>kaṣāyas</s>); the vows and the like [serve as stoppage].

children.text: § 806. yathā mahārṇave nāvo vivarapidhāne ’sati kramāt sratajalābhiplave sati tadāśrayāṇāṃ vināśo ’vaśyaṃbhāvī,

chidrapidhāne ca nirupadravam abhilaṣitadeśāntaraprāpaṇaṃ, tathā karmāgamadvārasaṃvaraṇe sati nāsti śreyaḥpratibandha iti saṃvaraguṇānucintanaṃ saṃvarānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya cintayataḥ saṃvare nityodyuktatā bhavati. tataś ca niḥśreyasapadaprāptir iti.
children.translated_text: but when the breach is sealed, there is safe and untroubled arrival at the desired destination — so too, when the doors of karmic influx are blocked, there is no obstruction to the highest good: such contemplation of the virtues of stoppage is the <s>saṃvarānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on stoppage). For when one thus reflects, one becomes constantly zealous in <s>saṃvara</s>. And from that follows the attainment of the state of supreme good.
Section 806. Just as in a great ocean, when the breach of a ship is not sealed, the gradual flooding by incoming water inevitably brings about the destruction of those aboard,

children.text: § 807. nirjarā vedanāvipāka ity uktam. sā dvedhā — abuddhipūrvā kuśalamūlā ceti. tatra narakādiṣu karmaphalavipākajā abuddhipūrvā sā akuśalānubandhā. pariṣahajaye kṛte kuśalamūlā sā śubhānubandhā niranubandhā ceti. ity evaṃ nirjarāyā guṇadoṣabhāvanaṃ nirjarānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asyānusmarataḥ karmanirjarāyai pravṛttir bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 807. <s>Nirjarā</s> (shedding) has been described as the fruition of experience (<s>vedanāvipāka</s>). It is twofold: that which is not preceded by wisdom (<s>abuddhipūrvā</s>) and that which has a wholesome root (<s>kuśalamūlā</s>). Of these, that which arises from the fruition of karmic results in the hells and other [destinies], not preceded by wisdom, is linked to unwholesomeness. That which results from the conquest of hardships (<s>pariṣahajaya</s>), having a wholesome root, is linked to auspiciousness or is without [further karmic] linkage. Thus the contemplation of the merits and faults of <s>nirjarā</s> is the <s>nirjarānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on shedding). For when one thus reflects, effort is directed toward the shedding of <s>karma</s>.

children.text: § 808. lokasaṃsthānādividhir vyākhyātaḥ samantād anantasyālokākāśasya bahumadhyadeśabhāvino lokasya saṃsthānādividhir vyākhyātaḥ. tatsvabhāvānucintanaṃ lokānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asyādhyavasyatas tattvajñānaviśuddhir bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 808. The arrangement of the universe's structure and the like has been explained — the structure and arrangement of the universe (<s>loka</s>), which occupies the central region of the infinite non-universe space (<s>alokākāśa</s>) extending in all directions. The contemplation of its nature is the <s>lokānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on the universe). For when one thus reflects, purification of the knowledge of reality occurs.

children.text: § 809. ekasmin nigotaśarīre jīvāḥ siddhānām anantaguṇāḥ. evaṃ sarvaloko nirantaraṃ nicitaḥ sthāvarair atas tatra trasatā vālukāsamudre patitā vajrasikatākaṇikeva durlabhā. tatra ca vikalendriyāṇāṃ bhūyiṣṭhatvāt pañcendriyatā guṇeṣu kṛtajñateva kṛcchralabhyā. tatra ca tiryaṃkṣu paśumṛgapakṣisarīsṛpādiṣu bahuṣu satsu manuṣyabhāvaś catuṣpathe ratnarāśir iva durāsadaḥ. tatpracyave ca punas tadutpattir dagdhatarupudgalatadbhāvopapattivad durlabhā. tallābhe ca deśakulendriyasaṃpannīrogatvāny uttarottaratto ’tidurlabhāni. sarveṣv api teṣu labdheṣu saddharmapratilambho yadi na syād vyarthaṃ janma vadanam iva dṛṣṭivikalam. tam evaṃ kṛcchalabhyaṃ dharmam avāpya viṣayasukhe rañjanaṃ bhasmārthacandanadahanam iva viphalam. viraktaviṣayasukhasya tu tapobhāvanādharmaprabhāvanāsukhamaraṇādilakṣaṇaḥ samādhir duravāpaḥ. tasmin sati bodhilābhaḥ phalavān bhavatīti cintanaṃ bodhidurlabhānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya bhāvayato bodhiṃ prāpya pramādo na kadācid api bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 809. In a single <s>nigoda</s> body, the souls are infinitely more numerous than the liberated ones. Thus the entire universe is densely packed without interruption with immobile beings (<s>sthāvaras</s>); among them, mobile existence (<s>trasatā</s>) is as rare as a diamond grain fallen in a desert of sand. And among the mobile, since those with incomplete senses are the majority, five-sensed existence is as difficult to obtain as gratitude among virtues. Among the five-sensed, since animals — beasts, deer, birds, reptiles, and the like — are numerous, the human state is as hard to reach as a heap of jewels at a crossroads. And upon departing from that [human state], rebirth in it again is as rare as the re-emergence of a burnt tree's material particles in that same form. Even upon obtaining it, the possession of [favorable] country, family, complete senses, and freedom from disease become progressively more and more difficult to obtain. And even when all of these are obtained, if the attainment of the true <s>dharma</s> does not occur, the birth is as futile as a face with defective vision. Having obtained this <s>dharma</s> that is so difficult to attain, to delight in sensual pleasure is as fruitless as burning sandalwood for the sake of ashes. And for one who has renounced sensual pleasure, the spiritual composure (<s>samādhi</s>) characterized by austerity, cultivation of contemplation, propagation of <s>dharma</s>, and peaceful death is hard to attain. When that is attained, the attainment of enlightenment (<s>bodhi</s>) bears fruit — such is the contemplation called <s>bodhidurlabhānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on the difficulty of attaining enlightenment). For when one thus contemplates, upon attaining <s>bodhi</s>, negligence never arises.

children.text: § 810. ayaṃ jinopadiṣṭo dharmo ’hiṃsālakṣaṇaḥ satyādiṣṭhito vinayamūlaḥ. kṣamābalo bhrahmacaryagupta upaśamapradhānī niyatilakṣaṇo niṣparigrahatālambanaḥ. asyālābhād anādisaṃsāre jīvāḥ paribhramanti duṣkarmavipākajaṃ duḥkham anubhavantaḥ. asya punaḥ pratilambhe vividhābhudayaprāptipūrvikā niḥśreyasopalabdir niyateti cintanaṃ dharmasvākhyātatvānuprekṣā. evaṃ hy asya cintayato dharmānurāgāt sadā pratiyatno bhavati.
children.translated_text: Section 810. This <s>dharma</s> taught by the <s>Jina</s> is characterized by non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>), founded on truth (<s>satya</s>) and the like, rooted in humility (<s>vinaya</s>), empowered by forbearance (<s>kṣamā</s>), guarded by celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), predominated by equanimity (<s>upaśama</s>), characterized by self-control (<s>niyati</s>), and supported by non-possessiveness (<s>niṣparigrahatā</s>). Due to the non-attainment of this [<s>dharma</s>], souls have been wandering in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, experiencing suffering born from the fruition of evil <s>karma</s>. Upon its attainment, however, the realization of supreme good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), preceded by the attainment of various kinds of prosperity, is certain — such contemplation is the <s>dharmasvākhyātatvānuprekṣā</s> (reflection on the well-proclaimed nature of <s>dharma</s>). For when one thus reflects, through devotion to <s>dharma</s>, constant effort is maintained.

children.text: § 811. evam anityatvādyanuprekṣāsaṃnidhāne uttamakṣamādidhāraṇān mahān saṃvaro bhavati. madhye ‘anuprekṣā’ vacanam ubhayārtham. anuprekṣā hi bhāvayann uttamakṣmādīṃś ca pratipālayati parīṣahāṃś ca jetum utsahate.
children.translated_text: Section 811. Thus, when contemplations on impermanence and the rest are present, along with the observance of supreme forbearance (<s>uttamakṣamā</s>) and the other [virtues], great <s>saṃvara</s> (stoppage of karmic influx) occurs. The word '<s>anuprekṣā</s>' (contemplation) is placed in the middle for a twofold purpose: for one who practices contemplation both upholds the supreme virtues beginning with forbearance and also becomes capable of conquering the hardships (<s>parīṣahas</s>).

children.text: § 812. ke punas te pariṣahāḥ kim arthaṃ vā te sahyanta itīdam āha —
children.translated_text: Section 812. What then are those hardships, and for what purpose are they to be endured? To this he says —

children.text: mārgācyavananirjarārthaṃ pariṣahoḍhavyāḥ parīṣahāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The <s>parīṣahas</s> (hardships) are to be endured for the sake of not falling from the path and for the sake of <s>nirjarā</s> (shedding of karma).

children.text: § 813. saṃvarasya prakṛtatvāt tena mārgo viśiṣyate. saṃvaramārga iti. tadacyavanārthaṃ nirjarārthaṃ ca pariṣoḍhavyāḥ parīṣahāḥ. kṣutpipāsādisahanaṃ kurvantaḥ jinopadiṣṭān mārgād apracyavamānās tanmārgaparikramaṇaparicayena karmāgamadvāraṃ saṃvṛṇvanta aupakramikaṃ karmaphalam anubhavantaḥ krameṇa nirjīrṇakarmāṇo mokṣam āpnuvanti.
children.translated_text: Section 813. Since <s>saṃvara</s> (stoppage) is the subject under discussion, the path is qualified by it — the path of <s>saṃvara</s>. The <s>parīṣahas</s> are to be endured for the sake of not falling from that [path] and for the sake of <s>nirjarā</s>. Those who practice endurance of hunger, thirst, and the rest, while not falling from the path taught by the <s>Jina</s>, through familiarity with the practice of that path, block the doors of karmic influx, experience the fruits of <s>karma</s> that has already commenced (<s>aupakramika</s>), and gradually, with <s>karma</s> shed away, attain <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).

children.text: § 814. tatsvarūpasaṃkhyāsaṃpratipattyartham āha —
children.translated_text: Section 814. In order to ascertain their nature and number, he says —

children.text: kṣutpipāsāśītoṣṇadaṃśamaśakanāgnyāratistrīcaryāniṣadyāśayyākrośavadhayācanālābharogatṛṇasparśamalasatkārapuraskāraprajñājñānādarśanāni ||
children.translated_text: Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insect bites, nakedness, ennui, women, wandering, sitting postures, sleeping places, abuse, assault, begging, non-obtaining, disease, contact with thorny grass, dirt, honor, reverence, learning, ignorance, and lack of faith.

children.text: § 815. kṣudādayo vedanāviśeṣā dvāviṃśatiḥ. eteṣāṃ sahanaṃ mokṣārthinā kartavyam. tad yathā — bhikṣor niravadyāhāragaveṣiṇas tadalābhe īṣallābhe ca anivṛttavedanasyākāle adeśe ca bhikṣāṃ prati nivṛtteccchasyāvaśyakaparihāṇiṃ manāg apy asahamānasya svādhyāyadhyānabhāvanāparasya bahukṛtvaḥ svakṛtaparakṛtānaśanāvam audaryasya nīrasāhārasya saṃtaptabhrāṣṭrapatitajalabindukatipayavatsahasā pariśuṣkapānasyodīrṇakṣudvedanasyāpi sato bhikṣālābhād alābham adhikaguṇaṃ manyamānasya kṣudbādhāṃ pratyacintanaṃ kṣudvijayaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 815. Hunger and the rest are twenty-two types of experiential afflictions. Their endurance must be practiced by one who seeks <s>mokṣa</s>. As follows: for a mendicant seeking blameless food, when it is not obtained, or when only a little is obtained, whose hunger is unrelenting, whose desire for alms has ceased at improper times and places, who does not tolerate even the slightest failure in his obligatory duties, who is devoted to self-study, meditation, and contemplation, who has many times observed fasts both self-imposed and imposed by others, who takes food devoid of flavor, whose drink is like a few drops of water fallen on a hot frying pan — quickly evaporating — and yet whose hunger-pangs have intensified: such a one considers the non-obtaining of alms as superior in merit to obtaining them, and his non-preoccupation with the affliction of hunger constitutes the conquest of hunger (<s>kṣudvijaya</s>).

children.text: § 816. jalasnānāvagāhanapariṣekaparityāginaḥ patatrivadaniyatāsanāvasathasyātilavaṇasnigdharūkṣaviruddhāhāragraiṣmātapapittajvarānaśanādibhir udīrṇāṃ śarīrendriyonmāthinīṃ pipāsāṃ pratyanādriyamāṇapratīkārasya pipāsānalaśikhāṃ dhṛtinavamṛdghaṭapūritaśītalasugandhisamādhivāriṇā praśamayataḥ pipāsāsahanaṃ praśasyate.
children.translated_text: Section 816. For one who has renounced bathing, immersion, and sprinkling with water, whose dwelling and seat are unfixed like a bird's, whose thirst has been intensified by excessively salty, oily, harsh, or unwholesome food, by summer's heat, bile-fever, fasting, and the like — raging through the body and senses — who disregards all remedies, who quenches the flames of thirst with the cool, fragrant water of <s>samādhi</s> (spiritual composure) stored in the fresh earthen vessel of fortitude — the endurance of such thirst is praised.

children.text: § 817. parityaktapracchādanasya pakṣivadanavadhāritālayasya vṛkṣamūlapathiśilātalādiṣu himānīpatanaśītalānilasaṃpāte tatpratikāraprāptiṃ prati nivṛttecchasya pūrvānubhūtaśītapratikārahetuvastūnām asmarato jñānabhāvanāgarbhāgāre vasataḥ śītavedanāsahanaṃ parikīrtyate.
children.translated_text: Section 817. For one who has renounced covering, whose shelter is unfixed like a bird's, who dwells at the foot of trees, roadsides, rock surfaces, and the like, amidst falling frost, cold winds, and their onslaught — whose desire for obtaining protection against these has ceased, who does not recall the objects that formerly served as remedies for cold previously experienced, who dwells in the inner chamber of the cultivation of knowledge (<s>jñānabhāvanā</s>) — the endurance of the sensation of cold is extolled.

children.text: § 818. nivāte nirjale grīṣmaravikiraṇapariśuṣkapatitaparṇavyapetacchāyātaruṇyaṭavyantare yadṛcchayopanipatitasyānaśanādyabhyantarasādhanotpāditadāhasya davāgnidāhaparuṣavātātapajanitagalatāluśoṣasya tatpratīkārahetūn bahūn anubhūtān acintayataḥ prāṇipīḍāparihārāvahitacetasaś cāritrarakṣaṇam uṣṇasahanam ity upavarṇyate.
children.translated_text: Section 818. For one who has by chance arrived in the interior of a forest devoid of shade, whose young trees have lost their leaves dried up and fallen by the rays of the summer sun, a place without wind and without water; whose body burns from the internal heat produced by inner practices such as fasting; whose throat and palate are parched by forest fire, harsh winds, and scorching heat; who does not think of the many previously experienced remedies for that [suffering]; and whose mind is attentive to avoiding injury to living beings — enduring heat for the sake of protecting one's conduct is described as the tolerance of the heat-affliction (<s>uṣṇapariṣaha</s>).

children.text: § 819. ‘daṃśamaśaka’ grahaṇam upalakṣaṇam. yathā
kākebhyo rakṣyatāṃ sarpiḥ
children.translated_text: 'Let the ghee be protected from crows' —

children.text: iti upaghātakopalakṣaṇaṃ kākagrahaṇaṃ, tena daṃśamaśakamakṣikāpiśukaputtikāmatkuṇakīṭapipīlikāvṛścikādayo gṛhyante. tatkṛtāṃ bādhāmapratīkārāṃ sahamānasya teṣāṃ bādhāṃ tridhāpyakurvāṇasya nirvāṇaprāptimātrasaṃkalpaprāvaraṇasya tadvedanāsahanaṃ daṃśamaśakapariṣahakṣamety ucyate.
children.translated_text: here the mention of 'crow' is illustrative of all agents of harm; by that, gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, gnats, wasps, bedbugs, beetles, ants, scorpions, and the like are included. For one who endures the affliction caused by them without remedy, who does not retaliate against their harm in any of the three ways [body, speech, mind], and whose only resolve is covered by the aspiration for <s>nirvāṇa</s> — the endurance of that suffering is called the conquest of the gadfly-and-mosquito affliction (<s>daṃśamaśakapariṣahakṣamā</s>).
Section 819. The mention of 'gadflies and mosquitoes' (<s>daṃśamaśaka</s>) is illustrative. Just as —

children.text: § 820. jātarūpavanniṣkalaṃkajātarūpadhāraṇamaśakyaprārthanīyaṃ yācanarakṣaṇahiṃsanādidoṣavinirmuktaṃ niṣparigrahatvān nirvāṇaprāptiṃ pratyekaṃ sādhanam ananyabādhanaṃ nāgnyaṃ bibhrato manovikriyāviplutivirahāt strīrūpāṇy atyantāśucikuṇaparūpeṇa bhāvayato rātrindivaṃ brahmacaryam akhaṇḍam ātiṣṭhamānasyācelavratadhāraṇam anavadyam avagantavyam.
children.translated_text: Section 820. Like gold — stainless as refined gold, worthy of desires that cannot be entreated, free from faults such as begging, guarding, and harming — being without possessions, each [practice] individually being a means to the attainment of <s>nirvāṇa</s>, not causing harm to others; for one who bears no garment (<s>acela</s>), who is free from mental disturbance and agitation, who contemplates female forms as utterly impure and repulsive, who maintains unbroken celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>) day and night — the observance of the vow of nudity (<s>acelavrata</s>) should be understood as blameless.

children.text: § 821. saṃyatasyendriyeṣṭaviṣayasaṃbandhaṃ prati nirutsakasya gītanṛtyavāditrādivirahiteṣu śūnyāgāradevakulatarukoṭaraśilāguhādiṣu svādhāyadhyānabhāvanāratim āskandato dṛṣṭaśrutānubhūtaratismaraṇatatkathāśravaṇakāmaśarapraveśanirvivarahṛdayasya prāṇiṣu sadā sadayasyāratipariṣahajayo ’vaseyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 821. For one who is restrained and indifferent toward the connection of the senses with desired objects; who delights in self-study, meditation, and contemplation in empty houses, temples, tree hollows, rock caves, and the like, devoid of song, dance, and music; whose heart is without any opening for the entry of the arrows of desire through the recollection of previously seen, heard, or experienced pleasures and hearing stories about them; who is always compassionate toward living beings — the conquest of the affliction of discontent (<s>aratipariṣaha</s>) should be understood.

children.text: § 822. ekānteṣv ārāmabhavanādipradeśeṣu navayauvanamadavibhramamadirāpānapramattāsu pramadāsu bādhamānāsu kūrmavatsaṃvṛtendriyavikārasya lalitasmitamṛdukathitasavilāsavīkṣaṇaprahasanamadamantharagamanamanmathaśaravyāpāraviphalīkaraṇasya strībādhāpariṣahanam avagantavyam.
children.translated_text: Section 822. In secluded places such as gardens and buildings, when young women intoxicated by the pride of youth and inebriated by wine press upon [the ascetic] — for one who, like a tortoise, has withdrawn sensory disturbances; who renders futile the operations of <s>Manmatha's</s> (Cupid's) arrows — namely, graceful smiles, soft speech, coquettish glances, laughter, the slow gait of intoxication — the endurance of the women-affliction (<s>strībādhāpariṣaha</s>) should be understood.

children.text: § 823. dīrghakālam uṣitagurukulabrahmacaryasyādhigatabandhamokṣapadārthatattvasya saṃyamāyatanabhaktihetor deśāntarātither guruṇābhyanujñātasya pavanavanniḥsaṃgatām aṅgīkurvato bahuśo ’naśanāvamaudaryavṛttiparisaṃkhyānarasaparityāgādibādhāpariklāntakāyasya deśakālapramāṇāpetam adhvagamanaṃ saṃyamavirodhi pariharato nirākṛtapādāvaraṇasya paruṣaśarkarākaṇṭakādivyadhanajātacaraṇakhedasyāpi sataḥ pūrvocitayānavāhanādigamanam asmarato yathākālam āvaśyakāparihāṇimāskandataś caryāpariṣahasahanam avaseyam.
children.translated_text: Section 823. For one who has long observed celibacy in the teacher's household, who has comprehended the reality of the categories of bondage and liberation, who wanders to other lands out of devotion to the abode of self-restraint, who has been permitted by the teacher, who accepts detachment like the wind; whose body is exhausted by the hardships of frequent fasting, reduced intake, regulated eating, renunciation of flavors, and the like; who avoids traveling distances disproportionate to place, time, and capacity as being contrary to self-restraint; who has discarded foot-coverings and whose feet suffer from harsh gravel, thorns, and the like, yet does not recall formerly accustomed conveyances such as vehicles and mounts; and who attends to the obligatory duties at the proper time without fail — the endurance of the wandering-affliction (<s>caryāpariṣaha</s>) should be understood.

children.text: § 824. smaśānodyānaśūnyāyatanagiriguhāgahvarādiṣv anabhyastapūrveṣu nivasata ādityaprakāśasvendriyajñānaparīkṣitapradeśe kṛtaniyamakriyasya niṣadyāṃ niyamitakālām āsthitavataḥ siṃhavyāghrādivividhabhīṣaṇadhvaniśravanān nivṛttabhayasya caturvidhopasargasahanād apracyutamokṣamārgasya vīrāsanotkuṭikādyāsanād avicalitavigrahasya tatkṛtabādhān sahanaṃ niṣadyāpariṣahavijaya iti niścīyate.
children.translated_text: Section 824. For one dwelling in previously unfrequented places such as cremation grounds, gardens, deserted buildings, mountain caves, and ravines; who has performed the prescribed ritual at a spot examined by sunlight and one's own sensory knowledge; who observes a seated posture (<s>niṣadyā</s>) for a regulated duration; who has overcome fear upon hearing the various terrifying sounds of lions, tigers, and the like; whose path to liberation is unshaken despite enduring the four types of calamities (<s>upasargas</s>); whose body is unmoved in postures such as the heroic seat (<s>vīrāsana</s>) and the squatting position (<s>utkuṭika</s>) — the endurance of the afflictions caused by that is determined as the conquest of the seated-posture affliction (<s>niṣadyāpariṣaha</s>).

children.text: § 825. svādhyāyadhyānādhvaśramaparikheditasya mauhūrtikīṃ kharaviṣam apracuraśarkarākapālasaṃkaṭātiśītoṣṇeṣu bhūmipradeśeṣu nidrām anubhavato yathākṛtaikaparśvadaṇḍāyitādiśāyinaḥ prāṇibādhāparihārāya patitadāruvad vyapagatāsuvadaparivartamānasya jñānabhāvanāvahitacetaso ’nuṣṭhitavyantarādivividhopasargād apy acalitavigrahasyāniyamitakālāṃ tatkṛtabādhāṃ kṣamamāṇasya śayyā pariṣahakṣamā kathyate.
children.translated_text: Section 825. For one exhausted by the labor of self-study, meditation, and travel; who experiences momentary sleep — harsh and brief — on ground surfaces that are rough with gravel and potsherds, excessively cold or hot; who sleeps in the prescribed manner lying on one side, straight as a staff; who, for the sake of avoiding harm to living beings, remains without turning, like a fallen log or one devoid of breath; whose mind is attentive to the contemplation of knowledge; whose body remains unmoved even from various calamities caused by <s>vyantara</s> (intermediary) beings and others — for one who endures afflictions of unregulated duration, the tolerance of the sleep-affliction (<s>śayyāpariṣaha</s>) is described.

children.text: § 826. mithyādarśanodṛiktāmarṣaparuṣāvajñānindāsabhyavacanāni krodhāgniśikhāpravardhanāni niśṛṇvato ’pi tadartheṣv asamāhitacetasaḥ sahasā tatpratīkāraṃ kartum api śaknuvataḥ pāpakarmavipākam abhicintayatas tāny ākarṇya tapaścaraṇabhāvanāparasya kaṣāyaviṣalavamātrasyāpy anavakāśam ātmahṛdayaṃ kurvata ākrośapariṣahasahanam avadhāryate.
children.translated_text: Section 826. Even while hearing words of anger, harshness, contempt, censure, and abuse arising from the arrogance of wrong faith — words that fuel the flames of anger — for one whose mind is not engaged with the content of those [words]; who, though capable of instantly retaliating, instead contemplates the fruition of sinful <s>karma</s>; who, upon hearing them, is devoted to the practice of austerity and contemplation; who makes his own heart give no room even for the slightest vomiting of the poison of passions (<s>kaṣāya</s>) — the endurance of the abuse-affliction (<s>ākrośapariṣaha</s>) is ascertained.

children.text: § 827. niśitaviśasanamuśalamudgarādripraharaṇatāḍanādibhir vyāpādyamānaśarīrasya vyāpādakeṣu manāg api manovikāram akurvato mama purākṛtaduṣkarmaphalam idam ime varākāḥ kiṃ kurvanti, śarīram idaṃ jalabudbudvadviśaraṇasvabhāvaṃ vyasanakāraṇam etair bābādhyate, saṃjñānadarśanacāritrāṇi mama na kenacid upahanyante iti cintayato vāsitakṣaṇacandanānulepanasamadarśino vadhapariṣahakṣamā manyate.
children.translated_text: Section 827. For one whose body is being destroyed by blows from sharp butchering implements, pestles, hammers, stones, and other weapons; who does not produce even the slightest mental disturbance toward those who would kill him [thinking]: 'This is the fruit of my previously committed evil <s>karma</s>; what can these wretched ones do? This body, whose nature is to disintegrate like a water bubble, is the cause of misfortune — it is being afflicted by them. My knowledge, perception, and conduct cannot be harmed by anyone'; who regards [the blows] equally with the application of sandal paste fragrant for an instant — the tolerance of the killing-affliction (<s>vadhapariṣaha</s>) is considered [to be this].

children.text: § 828. bāhyābhyantaratapo ’nuṣṭhānaparasya tadbhāvanāvaśena nissārīkṛtamūrteḥ paṭutapanatāpaniṣpītasārataror iva virahitacchāyasya tvagasthiśirājālamātratanuyantrasya prāṇātyaye saty apy āhārabasatibheṣajādīni dīnābhidhānamukhavaivarṇyāṅgasaṃjñādibhir ayācamānasya bhikṣākāle ’pi vidyududyotavad durupalakṣyamūrter yācanāpariṣahasahanam avasīyate.
children.translated_text: Section 828. For one devoted to the practice of external and internal austerities; whose body has been rendered insubstantial through the power of those contemplations, like a tree whose essence has been drained by the sharp heat of a burning fire, devoid of shade; whose body is a mere mechanism of skin, bones, and a network of sinews; who, even when life is in danger, does not beg for food, shelter, medicine, and the like through pitiful speech, change of countenance, gestures, or the like; whose form is scarcely perceptible even at mealtimes, like a flash of lightning — the endurance of the begging-affliction (<s>yācanāpariṣaha</s>) is determined.

children.text: § 829. vāyuvadasaṅgād anekadeśacāriṇo ’bhupagataikakālasaṃbhojanasya vācaṃyamasya tatsamitasya vā sakṛtsvatanudarśanamātratantrasya pāṇipuṭamātrapātrasya bahuṣu divaseṣu bahuṣu ca gṛheṣu bhikṣām anavāpyāpy asaṃkliṣṭacetaso dātṛviśeṣaparīkṣānirutsukasya lābhād apy alābho me paramaṃ tapa iti saṃtuṣṭasyālābhavijayo ’vaseyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 829. For one who, like the wind, wanders unattached through many regions; who has undertaken eating at a single time only; who observes silence or careful speech; whose [alms-collection] depends solely on a single glance at his own body [to determine need]; whose vessel is merely the cupped palms; who, even after not obtaining alms at many houses over many days, remains with an unafflicted mind; who is without eagerness to examine the particular qualities of the donor; who is content [thinking] 'Non-obtaining is for me the supreme austerity, even more than obtaining' — the conquest of the non-obtaining affliction (<s>alābhapariṣaha</s>) should be understood.

children.text: § 830. sarvāśucinidhānam idam anityam aparitrāṇam iti śarīre niḥsaṃkalpatvād vigatasaṃskārasya guṇaratnabhāṇḍasaṃcayapravardhanasaṃrakṣaṇasaṃdhāraṇakāraṇatvād abhyupagatasthitividhānasyākṣamrakṣaṇavad vraṇānulepanavad vā bahūpakāram āhāram abhupagacchato viruddhāhārapānasevanavaiṣamyajanitavātādivikārarogasya yugapad anekaśatasaṃkhyavyādhiprakope saty api tadvaśavartitāṃ vijahato jallauṣadhiprāptyādyanekatapoviśeṣarddhiyoge saty api śarīranisspṛhatvāt tatpratikārānapekṣiṇo rogapariṣahasahanam avagantavyam.
children.translated_text: Section 830. Because of having no attachment to the body, [regarding it as] 'This is a repository of all impurities, impermanent, and without protection' — for one who has abandoned [bodily] embellishment; who has adopted the prescribed regimen because [the body] serves as the cause for accumulating, increasing, protecting, and maintaining the treasure of virtuous qualities — like guarding the eyes [from disease] or like applying ointment to a wound — and thus takes food as greatly beneficial; who, though afflicted with diseases of wind and the like caused by improper food, drink, and imbalanced diet, and even when hundreds of ailments simultaneously flare up, does not submit to their control; who, even when there is the possibility of special austerity-powers such as obtaining healing herbs and the like, has no desire for the body and does not seek remedies — the endurance of the disease-affliction (<s>rogapariṣaha</s>) should be understood.

children.text: § 831. tṛṇagrahanam upalakṣaṇaṃ kasyācid vyadhanaduḥkhakāraṇasya. tena śuṣkatṛṇaparuṣaśarkarākaṇṭakaniśitamṛttikāśūlādivyadhanakṛtapādavedanāprāptau satyāṃ tatrāpraṇihitatacetasaś caryāśayyāniṣadyāsu prāṇipīḍāparihāre nityam apramattacetasas tṛṇādisparśabādhāpariṣahavijayo veditavyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 831. The mention of 'grass' (<s>tṛṇa</s>) is illustrative of anything that causes piercing pain. By that, dry grass, rough gravel, thorns, sharp earth clods, spikes, and the like are included. When pain in the feet arises from being pierced by these, for one whose mind is not directed toward that [pain], and who is always vigilant with an alert mind to avoid injury to living beings during walking, sleeping, and sitting — the conquest of the grass-contact affliction (<s>tṛṇasparśapariṣaha</s>) should be known.

children.text: § 832. apkāyikajantupīḍāparihārāyāmaraṇād asnānavratadhāriṇaḥ paṭur avikiraṇapratāpajanitaprasvedāktapavanānītapāṃsunicayasya sidhmakacchūdadrūdīrṇakaṇḍūyāyām utpannāyām api kaṇḍūyanavimardanasaṃghaṭṭanavivarjitamūrtheḥ svagatamalopacayaparagatamalāpacayayor asaṃkalpitamanasaḥ sajjñānacāritravimalasalilaprakṣālanena karmamalapaṃkanirākaraṇāya nityam udyatamater malapīḍāsahanam ākhyāyate.
children.translated_text: Section 832. For one who, to avoid injury to water-bodied creatures, observes the vow of not bathing until death; whose body is covered with accumulated dust brought by the wind and generated by the intense heat that evaporates perspiration without the cloth being spread out; who, even when itching arises from skin diseases such as <s>sidhmaka</s> (leucoderma), <s>kacchū</s> (scabies), and <s>dadrū</s> (ringworm), abstains from scratching, rubbing, and contact; whose mind is not occupied with either the accumulation of dirt on oneself or the removal of dirt on others; who is always intent on washing away the dirt of <s>karma</s>-mud with the pure water of right knowledge and right conduct — the endurance of the filth-affliction (<s>malapariṣaha</s>) is described.

children.text: § 833. satkāraḥ pūjāpraśaṃsātmakaḥ. puraskāro nāma kriyārambhādiṣv agrataḥ karaṇam āmaṃtraṇaṃ vā, tatrānādaro mayi kriyate. ciroṣitabrahmacaryasya mahātapasvinaḥ svaparasamayanirṇajñasya bahukṛtvaḥ paravādivijayinaḥ praṇāmabhaktisaṃbrahmāsanapradānādīni me na kaścit karoti.

mithyādṛṣṭaya evātīva bhaktim antaḥ kiṃcid ajānantam api sarvajñasaṃbhāvanayā saṃmānya svasamayaprabhāvanaṃ kurvanti. vyantarādayaḥ purā atyugratapasāṃ pratyagrapūjāṃ nirvartayantīti mithyā śrutir yadi na syād idānīṃ kasmān mādṛśāṃ na kurvantīti duṣpraṇidhānavirahitacittasya satkārapuraskārapariṣahavijaya iti vijñāyate.
children.translated_text: Those of wrong faith show excessive devotion, honoring even one who knows little internally, with the esteem due to an omniscient being, and thereby promote their own doctrine. [The thought arises:] '<s>Vyantara</s> (intermediary) beings and others formerly performed unprecedented worship for those of extremely fierce austerity — if that report is not false, why do they not do so now for one such as me?' — for one whose mind is free from such wrongful aspirations, the conquest of the honor-and-distinction affliction (<s>satkārapuraskārapariṣaha</s>) is understood.

Section 833. <s>Satkāra</s> (honor) consists of worship and praise. <s>Puraskāra</s> (distinction) means being placed first in the commencement of activities, or being invited [to lead]. When disregard is shown toward oneself [the ascetic reflects]: 'I have observed celibacy for a long time, I am a great ascetic, I am an expert in both my own and others' doctrines, I have defeated opponents many times — yet no one offers me salutation, devotion, respectful rising, or a seat.'

children.text: § 834. aṅgapūrvaprakīrṇakaviśāradasya śabdanyāyādhyātmanipuṇasya mama purastāditare bhāskaraprabhābhibhūtakhadyotodyotavannitarāṃ nāvabhāsanta iti vijñānamadanirāsaḥ prajñāpariṣahajayaḥ pratyetavyaḥ.
children.translated_text: Section 834. [The thought may arise:] 'I am learned in the <s>Aṅgas</s>, <s>Pūrvas</s>, and <s>Prakīrṇakas</s>; I am skilled in grammar, logic, and spiritual science — before me, others do not shine at all, like the glow of a firefly overwhelmed by the radiance of the sun.' The rejection of the pride of learning is to be recognized as the conquest of the wisdom-affliction (<s>prajñāpariṣaha</s>).
